dash.note5: Market cap / revenue in USD billions; '—' means data missing (e.g. LGD loss-making, no PE). Sentiment = short label of news sentiment + sell-side consensus.
dash.quad.ll.d: Cheap but sentiment is cold — pessimistic expectations may already be priced in (watch for value traps).
dash.quad.lr.d: Expensive and sentiment turning cold — highest risk of a double whammy.
dash.quad.ul.d: Cheap valuation and well-regarded by the market — quality and price combined.
dash.quad.ur.d: Market is bullish and valuation is rich — more sensitive to disappointments (priced for perfection).
dash.sec1.note: Note: when a peer has fewer than 2 comparables, falls back to the full-sample median (valuation conclusion holds, but comparability is slightly lower).
dash.sec1.sub: Score = mean of (current valuation multiple ÷ peer median multiple): <0.85 undervalued (blue), 0.85–1.15 fair (green), >1.15 overvalued (red).
dash.sec2.sub: X-axis = relative valuation score (right = more expensive); Y-axis = sentiment index (news + sell-side consensus, -1 bearish ~ +1 bullish); bubble size = market cap (USD billions).
dash.sec3.sub: Shares of news sentiment (media/events) and sell-side analyst consensus (rating/target price).
dash.sec4.sub: X-axis = net margin; Y-axis = ROE; bubble size = revenue (TTM, USD billions); color = valuation verdict.

report.header.source: Data source: public supply-chain reports and teardowns (2024–2026, incl. Counterpoint / Nikkei / TrendForce / stockanalysis) + Apple's 2024 Supplier List (187 core suppliers, ~98% of direct spend); this report models 60 key suppliers, 27 core components, and 28 product models therefrom.
report.header.subtitle: Apple Product Supply-Chain Graph · Product Line × Component × Supplier × Supply Chain (attribute-enhanced v2)
report.header.title: Apple Product Supply-Chain Graph Report
report.intro.products: Covers six product lines — iPhone / Mac / iPad / Apple Watch / Vision Pro / AirPods·HomePod (sorted by release date).
report.intro.suppliers: Full name, English name, and short name are listed separately; tier=1 marks core / high-moat suppliers. Sorted by region.
report.limits.l1: Model coverage spans on-sale / announced mainstream models from 2020–2026 (earliest: HomePod mini, 2020), with status labeled; some not-yet-announced models (e.g., foldable iPhone) are forward-looking only and excluded from modeling.
report.limits.l2: Supplier shares are annotated only for the few segments with clear public disclosure (e.g., BOE 51% of MacBook panels, Samsung ~60–70% of DRAM); the rest are described qualitatively as 'major suppliers' without per-item quantification.
report.limits.l3: Component–supplier mappings are based on public teardowns / BOMs and supply-chain reporting, reflecting mainstream configurations; different batches / regions of the same model may have second-source differences.
report.limits.l4: Alias records only publicly credible pre-announcement codenames or nicknames, left blank if none; release dates follow announcement / launch dates, with the year noted for unconfirmed models.
report.limits.l5: Data is for industry-structure research and education, and constitutes no investment or procurement advice.
report.model.intro: The graph uses four node tiers and five relationship types, fully reflecting the upstream–downstream path plus assembly / mass-production links:
report.model.l0: Tier 0 — End Products (Product): down to the specific model, e.g., iPhone 17 Pro, MacBook Pro 14″ (M4), Apple Vision Pro (M5); with attributes such as release date, status, and starting price.
report.model.l1: Tier 1 — Core Components (Component): SoC, display panels, CIS, lenses, memory, modems, PMIC, batteries, mechanical parts, FPC/substrate, advanced packaging, etc.; with Chinese and English names.
report.model.l2: Tier 2 — Suppliers / Contract Manufacturers (Supplier): categorized into foundry, display, memory, semiconductor, acoustics, mechanical, FPC/substrate, OSAT, assembly, etc.; full/English/short names listed separately; tier=1 marks core / high-moat suppliers, tier=2 marks secondary / more substitutable ones.
report.risk.note: The shares and dates above (BOE panel 51%, Samsung DRAM ~60–70%, Sony CIS monopoly, Japanese components >60% in camera, TSMC Arizona only legacy A16, Amkor US plant ~2028, etc.) are drawn from public teardowns and market research (Counterpoint / Nikkei / TrendForce / stockanalysis) and vendor disclosures, reflecting mainstream configurations of 2025–2026; they may change over time and are provided for supply-chain structure research only.
report.risk.r1: Single-point foundry dependency (TSMC / Taiwan): the most advanced chips such as A19 / A19 Pro / M-series are 100% fabricated by TSMC's Taiwan fabs (3nm N3E/N3P), and advanced nodes are legally barred from moving offshore. Geopolitical risk is highly concentrated; the Arizona plant currently handles only older A16 and packaging.
report.risk.r2: Single-point image-sensor dependency (Sony / Japan): iPhone main-camera CIS is exclusively Sony's; Japanese parts exceed 60% of a single iPhone camera module, making short-term substitution difficult (Samsung is only a potential future second source).
report.risk.r3: Display duopoly (Samsung Display / LG Display): OLED is led by Korean makers; BOE is ramping fast in iPhone 17/17 Air and MacBook Air (51% of MacBook panel share), but high-end Pro models still rely mainly on Korean makers.
report.risk.r4: Tariffs and the 'China + N' reshuffle: U.S. tariffs on China push assembly to India/Vietnam, yet core components are still largely imported from East Asia (roughly 52% of an India iPhone's core components must be air-freighted from China), limiting the speed and yield of the shift.
report.risk.r5: Advanced-packaging gap: wafers from TSMC Arizona still require InFO/CoWoS advanced packaging in Asia; Amkor's U.S. plant is not expected to open until 2028, so a short-term closed loop is difficult.
report.risk.r6: Single-source component (single point of failure): the audio codec & haptics chip (audio_codec) is supplied by only Cirrus (Cirrus Logic) in this dataset — the sole single-point dependency; any supply disruption or yield issue would affect audio and haptics across the lineup, so secondary-supplier progress must be tracked closely.
report.summary.b1: High regional concentration: ~77% (46/60) of suppliers are headquartered in East Asia (incl. mainland China, Taiwan, Japan, Korea), with the manufacturing hub concentrated in mainland China and Taiwan; Sony (Japan) monopolizes high-end CIS, Samsung/LG (Korea) lead OLED, and TSMC (Taiwan) exclusively fabricates the most advanced process nodes.
report.summary.b2: Multi-sourcing to hedge risk: almost every critical component has ≥2 suppliers (e.g., three for DRAM, five for NAND, three for OLED) to preserve bargaining power and supply resilience.
report.summary.b3: 'China + N' capacity shift: iPhone final assembly is moving to India, AirPods/Watch/Vision Pro to Vietnam, and some Mac production to Thailand/Malaysia, yet core precision components remain heavily dependent on East Asia.
report.summary.note: This (v2) release adds attributes: supplier nodes are split into three independent fields — full name / English name / short name; product nodes add English name, alias/codename, release date, status, and starting price; component nodes add an English name. See the project doc 'Data Model & Field Dictionary' for field meanings and availability.
report.summary.p1: Starting from concrete product models, this report traces upstream to the core components (SoC, display panels, image sensors, memory, modems, batteries, mechanical parts, packaging, etc.) and their suppliers / contract manufacturers, building a three-tier 'Product → Component → Supplier' directed graph. risk.formulaComp: Formula: V = 1 / n (n = # suppliers; n = 1 means single point, V = 1.0)
risk.formulaProd: Formula: V = 0.5 × mean + 0.3 × weakest + 0.2 × single-point rate
